subtitle: ADA Title II includes a rule for public web content, and leaders need to know both what it covers and where its limits are. Plan accessible documents and services with the right expertise involved.
scope: For DHS leaders responsible for public web content, documents and mobile services. This course distinguishes ADA Title II public-service duties from employment accommodation and Minnesota’s existing digital standard. Formal exception, burden and legal decisions belong to authorized agency officials.
introTranscript: A person should be able to find information, complete an online task and use a public service with effective access. The ADA Title II web rule sets a technical standard for state and local government web content and mobile apps. It also contains specific exceptions and limits that need careful reading. This course explains the rule through a practice DSD service page, its documents and a contracted form. You will identify what is covered, use the current compliance dates correctly, examine an exception without overstating it, and plan the work with accessibility and legal colleagues. A later federal date does not pause Minnesota’s existing standard or the obligation to respond to a person’s access need.

lessons.title: See the complete public service
lessons.summary: The web rule covers content and apps the public entity provides, including services provided through arrangements with others.
lessons.objective: Identify a public webpage, document and contracted service that need to be included in a review.
objectives: Identify a public webpage, document and contracted service that need to be included in a review.
Distinguish public-service accessibility from an employee accommodation request.
Map a complete online task rather than reviewing only its front page.
takeaways: Review the information, linked documents and actions that make up the service.
A contractor does not automatically remove the public entity’s web responsibility.
Title II public-service duties and employment accommodation use different processes.
lessons.statement: A public service can cross several pages and providers. The person experiences one task, not your organizational boundaries.

image.caption: Connected information and tools should support one usable path through the service.

intro.heading: Include the steps people actually use
intro.body:
A practice DSD service page explains a waiver program, links to a document and directs a person to a vendor-hosted form. The page may be readable while the document or form blocks a person who uses a screen reader or keyboard. The review needs to include the full task. A usable introduction alone does not establish that the person can access the service.

Under 28 CFR 35.200, the rule covers web content and mobile apps a public entity provides or makes available directly or through contractual, licensing or other arrangements. The public entity cannot assume that a vendor-hosted form is outside the responsibility simply because the address or tool belongs to another company. Coordinate with procurement and accessibility staff to understand the arrangement and the actual service.

Keep the subject clear. Title II concerns state and local government services, programs and activities. An employee asking for a disability-related adjustment in their own job raises an employment accommodation question with its appropriate process. An internal tool may also be subject to Minnesota’s digital standard. Different responsibilities can overlap, but sending every question through the same procedure can delay a response.

As a leader, identify what people need to find, understand and do. Include sign-in, instructions, fields, errors, attachments and confirmation where relevant. Ask who owns each part and who can correct it. This inventory is a planning step, not a legal determination that every item has exactly the same requirements or that an exception applies. It gives the appropriate specialists a clear starting point and prevents a connected service from disappearing between teams.

inThisLesson: Include linked documents and contracted steps.
Identify owners for each part of the service.
lessons.keyStatement: Review the service as the person uses it, including the steps owned by another team or vendor.

flashcards.back: A state or local government entity covered by ADA Title II. The rule’s population and responsibility questions concern the entity, not merely a work unit.
Information and experience provided through the web, which can include documents and interactive tasks. Specific definitions and exceptions require careful review.
Content or an app provided through an arrangement with the public entity. The arrangement does not automatically remove its access responsibility.
All the steps required to obtain information, communicate a choice or complete an action, including confirmation and follow-up.

accordion.heading: What to include in the inventory

items.title: Information and attachments
items.body: Record public pages, linked documents and the purpose each serves. An older attachment may still be part of an active application process.

items.title: Actions and responses
items.body: Include the fields, errors, sign-in and confirmation needed to complete the task. These are often where a usable page leads to a blocked service.

items.title: Shared and contracted parts
items.body: Identify who can change vendor-hosted content and what the contract covers. Bring the appropriate procurement and accessibility staff into the review.

tabs.label: A resident’s online task
tabs.body: Review it as part of the public service under Title II and relevant state requirements. Respond to a present access need through the responsible process.

tabs.label: An employee’s request
tabs.body: Use the employment accommodation route when the employee needs a disability-related work adjustment. Do not make the public web deadline its response rule.

tabs.label: The agency’s digital standard
tabs.body: The Minnesota standard addresses state digital information and technology. Its current requirements remain relevant apart from a later federal deadline.

check.question: A public page links to a vendor-hosted application form provided under an agency contract. What is the sound review approach?
check.correct: Include the contracted form in the service review and coordinate with the responsible procurement and accessibility staff.
wrong: Exclude it automatically because it is hosted by a vendor.
Check only the public page title.
Tell the resident to contact the employee accommodation office for all form issues.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The rule includes provision through contractual and other arrangements. Review the actual task and coordinate responsibilities rather than assuming the hosting address removes them.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Follow the service path. A separate host or a readable headline does not establish that the person can complete the agency task.

items.text: The contracted application form linked from the agency page.
An employee asks for a disability-related adjustment to their work setup.
Who can correct the form’s confirmation step?
A document currently used to apply for the program.
An applicant requests an adjustment for an employment interview.
Which team and vendor contacts own each step?

lessons.next: The next lesson explains the current federal dates and why they are not a reason to pause existing access work.

scenario.context: In this example, a team says its vendor owns the application form, so only the agency’s introductory webpage needs attention. A resident reports that the form cannot be completed by keyboard.
options: Assume the report is outside agency responsibility.
Include the contracted step in the review, involve responsible staff and address the person’s current access need.
Remove the information page so nobody can find the service.
responses: A contractual arrangement does not automatically remove the public entity’s duty.
This follows the actual task and connects the current barrier to the appropriate response and correction process.
Removing a route without ensuring effective access can create another barrier. The need is to examine and address the service.

lessons.transfer: List the connected steps in a practice public service and identify which are owned by the agency, another team or a contractor.

move.control: You can make the whole service visible in the review.
move.failure: Only the agency-controlled front page is examined.
move.next: Create a task inventory and involve the owners of the linked or contracted steps.

lessons.title: Use the current dates without postponing access
lessons.summary: The federal dates changed in 2026. Minnesota’s existing digital standard and continuing ADA duties still matter.
lessons.objective: State the current federal compliance dates and the entity-size distinction.
objectives: State the current federal compliance dates and the entity-size distinction.
Explain why staff count or the size of one unit does not determine the public entity’s date.
Distinguish the federal timeline from Minnesota’s standard effective July 1, 2024.
takeaways: For entities of 50,000 or more, other than special districts, the current date is April 26, 2027.
For smaller entities and special district governments, the current date is April 26, 2028.
A later federal date does not cancel an existing state requirement or present access responsibility.
lessons.statement: A date tells you when a particular requirement applies. It does not erase responsibilities that already exist.

image.caption: Planning works best when the team uses current requirements rather than a remembered deadline.

intro.heading: Read the timeline in context
intro.body:
The 2024 federal web rule originally set earlier dates. A Department of Justice interim final rule effective April 20, 2026 extended them. Current 28 CFR 35.200 states April 26, 2027 for public entities with a total population of 50,000 or more, other than special district governments. It states April 26, 2028 for entities with a population below 50,000 and for special district governments. Old presentations may still display the earlier dates, so consult the current rule rather than relying on memory.

The population question concerns the public entity, not the number of staff on a team, people using one webpage or residents served by a single program. A small DHS work unit does not become a small public entity because it has fewer than 50,000 users. Minnesota is a state government with a population above that threshold. Use the responsible agency guidance for the entity and planning timeline; do not choose a later date from a unit’s staff count.

Minnesota’s State Digital Accessibility Standard version 4 took effect July 1, 2024. It adopts WCAG 2.1 A and AA and specified Section 508 requirements with state qualifications. A federal extension does not repeal that standard. Continuing Title II duties, including effective communication, also remain relevant before and after the technical-rule compliance date.

In the practice DSD project, the leader keeps accessible design, review and repair in the work plan rather than delaying them to the federal date. This is not about claiming every legal issue is already settled. It is about separating timelines and getting accurate guidance so a team does not turn one changed deadline into a blanket permission to ignore known barriers.

inThisLesson: Use the public entity’s population correctly.
Plan work without ignoring current barriers.
lessons.keyStatement: Use the current date for the correct entity, and continue the responsibilities that already apply.

flashcards.back: The date a particular rule’s specified requirements must be met. It is not a universal starting date for all disability access duties.
The public entity’s population under the rule’s definition, not a work unit’s staff or service-user count.
A category defined in the rule with the April 26, 2028 date. Do not assign this label to a unit without the appropriate basis.
Minnesota’s digital accessibility requirements effective July 1, 2024, separate from the revised federal timeline.

items.title: Using an old slide
items.body: A course or presentation may still show the 2024 rule’s original dates. Use the current federal text and official agency planning information.

items.title: Counting team members
items.body: The rule’s population test is about the public entity. The number of employees in a section does not move the agency into the smaller-entity category.

items.title: Pausing until the date
items.body: A federal extension does not cancel the Minnesota standard or a present need for effective communication and service access.

tabs.label: Federal rule
tabs.body: Current dates under §35.200 are April 26, 2027 and April 26, 2028 for the specified entity categories.

tabs.label: Minnesota standard
tabs.body: Version 4 is effective July 1, 2024. Its requirements remain applicable unless an appropriate state exemption or exception applies.

tabs.label: A person’s access need
tabs.body: The responsible agency process must address the current service and communication need. A future technical-rule date is not an automatic answer.

check.question: A DHS unit has 200 staff. Can it use the smaller-entity federal date solely for that reason?
check.correct: No. The rule uses the public entity’s total population, not the unit’s employee count.
wrong: Yes. Every unit with fewer than 50,000 staff receives the later date.
Yes. The number of visitors to one page determines the deadline.
No dates or standards apply before every document is inventoried.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Read the entity-size rule correctly. Minnesota’s state-government population and current agency guidance matter; a staff count does not determine the category.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Separate the entity’s population from team size and page use. Inventory supports planning but does not remove existing responsibilities.

items.text: April 26, 2027 applies to the specified 50,000-or-more entity category.
Minnesota standard version 4 is effective July 1, 2024.
A federal extension means known barriers can be ignored until 2027.
Smaller entities and special district governments have April 26, 2028 under the current rule.
State digital work still needs the relevant state accessibility review.
A section’s employee count determines the public entity’s population.

scenario.context: In this example, a manager finds an old slide giving April 24, 2026 as the larger-entity date. Another manager says the revised date allows the team to pause every access repair.
options: Use the old date because it appears in a familiar presentation.
Pause all work until the revised federal date.
Use the current federal rule and keep existing Minnesota requirements and present access needs in the plan.
responses: The federal dates were revised. Familiarity is not a reason to retain outdated timeline information.
The extension does not cancel the state standard or continuing responsibilities.
This separates the timelines accurately and preserves necessary work. Consult the responsible offices about specific planning questions.

move.control: You can use current authority and keep the timelines clear.
move.failure: A changed deadline becomes a blanket permission to postpone every responsibility.
move.next: Check the current rule and agency planning guidance before repeating a date.

lessons.title: Ask what accessible use requires
lessons.summary: WCAG 2.1 A and AA provides technical criteria. Leaders still need evidence about the complete configured task.
lessons.objective: Explain four broad accessibility principles in relation to a public task.
objectives: Explain four broad accessibility principles in relation to a public task.
Identify a visual-only or mouse-only design that needs review.
Distinguish a limited automated result from a complete conformance conclusion.
takeaways: People need to perceive information, operate the task, understand it and use it with relevant technology.
Clear writing and digital structure address different aspects of access.
A checker or product badge cannot establish every required criterion by itself.
lessons.statement: A technically useful question connects a requirement to what a person needs to do.

image.caption: A clean appearance is only one view of the information and its controls.

intro.heading: Translate the standard into task questions
intro.body:
WCAG stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. The federal rule adopts version 2.1 Level A and Level AA success criteria and conformance requirements. These are technical requirements, not a general promise that a site feels easy. Accessibility specialists interpret and test them. Leaders can make that work possible by asking concrete questions and providing the necessary time and authority.

The guidelines organize access around information that can be perceived, tasks that can be operated, content that can be understood and compatibility with user agents and assistive technologies. For a service form, ask whether someone can understand the field labels, reach controls by keyboard, recognize errors and know what happened after submission. For a document, ask about headings, reading order and meaningful alternatives to visual content. These questions illustrate the work; they are not the full technical checklist.

A practice notice uses red text alone to show a required action and includes an image of important instructions. A person who cannot distinguish that color or access the image’s meaning may miss the next step. A correction needs more than a cleaner visual layout. The author and specialist should provide accessible information and check the final format, including linked documents.

Automated tools can identify some issues, but cannot establish all criteria or complete task usability. A tagged PDF may still have incorrect reading order or meaningless headings. A vendor report may not cover the configured form or attachments. Ask what was examined, what remains and how the actual task was checked. Avoid declaring universal compliance from one successful test. A supported conclusion states its scope and sends unresolved questions to the responsible expertise.

inThisLesson: Connect broad principles to a real task.
Understand the limits of automated checks.
Ask for scoped evidence and follow-up.
lessons.keyStatement: Ask what a person can actually do, and what evidence supports that answer.

flashcards.back: The technical success criteria and conformance requirements adopted by the federal rule. The applicable standard is more specific than a general usability preference.
The ability to operate relevant controls without relying on a mouse, subject to the applicable technical criteria.
The sequence in which content is presented to assistive technology. A visually tidy page may still have an incorrect sequence.
A review that states the tasks, formats and criteria checked, along with what remains unexamined.

items.title: Task evidence
items.body: Ask whether the person can complete the relevant action, including correcting an error and receiving confirmation. A page-by-page visual check may miss this.

items.title: Technical evidence
items.body: Ask which requirements were examined and which specialists or tools were used. Automation is useful but only part of the evaluation.

items.title: Correction evidence
items.body: After a change, verify the final format and task. A source document may differ from its exported file or contracted display.

tabs.label: It looks clear
tabs.body: Appearance can help but does not establish keyboard operation, reading order or meaningful information for different ways of access.

tabs.label: The checker passed
tabs.body: A checker tests a limited set of issues. Ask what it cannot check and what manual or task review remains.

tabs.label: The task was tested
tabs.body: Useful evidence specifies the task, conditions and relevant criteria. It still needs a conclusion no broader than the review.

check.question: A PDF has tags and passes an automated check. What can the leader conclude?
check.correct: Those are useful steps, but reading order, meaning and other relevant checks still need verification before a complete conclusion.
wrong: The PDF necessarily meets every accessibility requirement.
No person should ever review the PDF manually.
The PDF can replace any accessible online form without further review.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Structure and automation can support access but do not establish every criterion or the whole task. Ask for the remaining evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Do not extend a limited result to universal conformance. The final document and its role in the service still need appropriate review.

items.text: A review records which form tasks worked with keyboard navigation.
The PDF has tags, so no other question matters.
Verify that the required action is not conveyed by color alone.
The specialist identifies the criteria checked and remaining limits.
The page is attractive, so it must work for assistive technology.
Check the exported document’s reading order and linked instructions.

lessons.next: The next lesson examines the rule’s narrow exceptions rather than treating all older content as exempt.

scenario.context: A practice notice passes an automated check but uses only a red color to show a required action. The team wants to publish based on the checker result.
scenario.prompt: What should the leader ask for?
options: Only a more attractive shade of red.
An appropriate review and correction of the information’s meaning and access, followed by checks of the final task.
A claim that the tool’s passing result overrides all technical criteria.
responses: A cosmetic color change does not necessarily give the action a meaningful non-color cue or address other requirements.
This connects the observed issue to the relevant review rather than overclaiming from automation.
The checker’s limits do not override the standard.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice form or document. Write two concrete access questions and one limit of the evidence you currently have.

move.control: You can request relevant task and technical evidence.
move.failure: A tag, badge or checker result is treated as complete proof.
move.next: Ask the responsible specialist what remains to be checked in the final service.

lessons.title: Read exceptions narrowly
lessons.summary: The rule names specific categories. A document’s age, an archive label or a contractor’s name does not automatically establish an exception.
lessons.objective: Explain why an older document currently used for service access is not covered by the preexisting-document exception.
objectives: Explain why an older document currently used for service access is not covered by the preexisting-document exception.
Identify the four conditions in the archived-web-content definition.
Distinguish independent third-party content from content posted through an arrangement with the public entity.
takeaways: Exceptions have conditions that need review.
An old application form in current use is not exempt under the preexisting-document category merely because it is old.
An exception to this subpart’s technical requirement does not erase other Title II duties or Minnesota requirements.
lessons.statement: An exception is a specific rule to examine, not a general label to put on inconvenient content.

image.caption: The purpose and present use of a document matter as much as its age.

intro.heading: Check the conditions, not just the label
intro.body:
The federal rule lists exceptions for defined archived web content, certain preexisting conventional electronic documents, independent third-party content, specified individualized secured documents and preexisting social media posts. Each category has boundaries. The appropriate accessibility and legal staff should interpret them alongside the agency’s other responsibilities. A leader should not mark a whole library exempt because some files are old.

The preexisting conventional-document exception does not include documents currently used to apply for, gain access to or participate in the public entity’s services, programs or activities. In the practice DSD task, a form created years ago is still the required application. Its age alone does not place it in that exception. An old flyer no longer used for current participation raises a different question and still needs the appropriate review.

Archived web content has four definition conditions: it was created before the applicable compliance date or reproduces qualifying physical or paper material; it is retained exclusively for reference, research or recordkeeping; it is not altered or updated after the date of archiving; and it is organized and clearly identified as archived. Simply placing an active form in a folder named Archive does not meet those conditions.

Content posted by an independent third party differs from content posted under contractual, licensing or other arrangements with the public entity. A contracted form is not automatically independent third-party content. Even when a specific exception applies to this subpart’s technical requirement, effective communication and other Title II duties continue, and Minnesota’s standard must be considered separately. Treat an exception conclusion as a reasoned authorized decision, not a shortcut around a known access need.

lessons.keyStatement: Age alone does not determine whether a document can remain outside the technical requirement.

flashcards.back: A limited category for qualifying conventional electronic documents, excluding documents currently used to apply for, access or participate in public services.

Content meeting all four definition conditions: qualifying creation or physical-source timing, exclusive reference/research/recordkeeping purpose, no alteration or update after the date of archiving, and dedicated clearly identified archive storage.
Content not posted because of a contractual, licensing or other arrangement with the public entity. The distinction requires attention to the actual arrangement.
A responsibility, such as effective communication, that is not erased by an exception to the web subpart’s technical rule.

items.title: Is the document active?
items.body: Ask whether people currently use it to apply for or take part in a service. A creation date does not answer that question.

items.title: Does the archive meet every condition?
items.body: Check the qualifying creation or physical-source timing, exclusive purpose, absence of alteration or update after the date of archiving, and dedicated clearly identified storage. A folder title alone cannot make active service material archived content.

items.title: What arrangement exists?
items.body: Determine whether another party acts independently or under an agency arrangement. Hosting and contractual responsibility are different questions.

tabs.label: An older application
tabs.body: Still required for current service access. Its age does not qualify it for the preexisting-document exception.

tabs.label: An historical report
tabs.body: May raise a genuine archived-content question if all definition conditions are met. Obtain appropriate review and keep continuing duties distinct.

tabs.label: A contracted form
tabs.body: Provided under the agency’s arrangement with a vendor. It is not automatically independent third-party content.

check.question: A PDF application was created years ago but is still used to apply for a current service. Does age alone put it in the preexisting-document exception?
check.correct: No. Documents currently used for application, access or participation are excluded from that exception.
wrong: Yes. Every old PDF is exempt.
Yes, if the team moves it to a folder called Archive.
Yes, if it is hosted by any vendor.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Current use matters. The exception has a specific boundary, and an active application is not exempt merely because of its age.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Review the purpose and conditions. Neither a folder name nor a host changes the active service use or automatically establishes an exception.

items.text: Every document made before the deadline is exempt forever.
Is the item retained exclusively for reference, research or recordkeeping?
Respond appropriately when a person needs effective communication.
A folder called Archive makes an active application exempt.
Was the content posted under a contractual arrangement with the public entity?
Consider Minnesota’s existing digital standard separately.

lessons.next: The next lesson considers present access and why a phone number or alternate version is not an automatic substitute for an accessible service.

scenario.context: In this example, a team puts its still-required application in an Archive folder and says it no longer needs attention under the federal rule.
options: Accept the folder name as sufficient proof.
Delete the application without providing another usable service route.
Review its current use and the actual exception conditions with appropriate staff; do not treat the label as a waiver.
responses: The definition has substantive conditions, and the document remains part of active participation.
Deletion alone may prevent service access. The team needs an effective route and a proper decision.
This examines the correct facts and keeps present service access and other requirements in view.

lessons.transfer: For a practice document, note its purpose, current use, updates and posting arrangement. Identify what the right person would need before considering an exception.

move.control: You can ask for a specific, supported exception analysis.
move.failure: Old age or an archive label replaces examining the conditions.
move.next: Bring the relevant facts to the responsible accessibility and legal staff.

lessons.title: Respond to a person’s present access need
lessons.summary: A technical timeline or exception does not answer every communication question. The person still needs an effective route to the service.
lessons.objective: Explain why a phone number does not automatically provide equivalent digital access.
objectives: Explain why a phone number does not automatically provide equivalent digital access.
Identify the narrow basis for a conforming alternate version under the web rule.
Describe a current access response that protects timeliness, privacy and independence.
takeaways: Consider whether the proposed route actually works for the person and context.
Conforming alternate versions are allowed under the rule only when direct access is not possible because of technical or legal limitations.
A future date or exception does not remove continuing effective-communication responsibilities.
lessons.statement: A workaround is useful only if it gives the person effective access, with the circumstances and remaining barrier taken seriously.

image.caption: People need a route that works for their task and communication needs, not an assumed substitute.

intro.heading: Ask whether the response is effective
intro.body:
A practice resident cannot use a service form. The team offers a phone number that is staffed for a short period each day and requires the caller to explain private information aloud. That may not provide an effective route for the person’s task. A phone option can be useful, but simply listing it does not establish accessibility, equivalent timing or privacy. The responsible staff need to examine the communication need and the service context.

ADA Title II’s effective-communication duties continue even where a particular web-rule exception applies or the technical compliance date has not yet arrived. The method depends on the circumstances and the person’s needs. Use the responsible agency process to arrange appropriate support, consider the person’s requested method and preserve meaningful control over the task. Do not assume a relative should handle private information because the digital route is inaccessible.

The web rule also limits the use of conforming alternate versions. Under §35.202, a public entity may use them to comply only when it is not possible to make the web content directly accessible because of technical or legal limitations. Convenience, cost preference or an inaccessible primary design is not automatically that basis. Equivalent facilitation is another provision requiring substantially equivalent or greater accessibility and usability, not a general promise that any alternative will do.

When a barrier is reported, connect the immediate response and the lasting correction. Describe what is currently available, who is responsible and what remains unresolved. Seek the appropriate specialist and legal guidance for formal questions. A course scenario cannot establish an exemption, but it can help a leader avoid treating a generic workaround as proof that the access question is finished.

inThisLesson: Evaluate the actual usefulness of a workaround.
Connect immediate access with lasting correction.
lessons.keyStatement: Do not call an alternative effective until its effect on the person’s task has been considered.

flashcards.back: Communication that works for the person and circumstances, with appropriate aids or services considered through Title II responsibilities.
A version meeting WCAG’s conditions whose use under the federal rule is limited to technical or legal inability to make the content directly accessible.
Alternative designs, methods or techniques that provide substantially equivalent or greater access and usability under the rule.
The person’s ability to conduct the task without unnecessary disclosure or imposed reliance on someone else. These are relevant to real access.

items.title: Can the person use it?
items.body: Ask whether the offered method fits the communication need and task. A phone option may help some people and be ineffective for others.

items.title: Can the task be completed in time?
items.body: Consider deadlines, hours and the actual transaction. A delayed route can create a different barrier even if the information eventually arrives.

items.title: What remains to be corrected?
items.body: An immediate response does not necessarily fix the recurring digital barrier. Assign ownership and verify the appropriate correction.

tabs.label: Telephone assistance
tabs.body: Potentially useful, but not an automatic proof of equal access. Consider effective communication, privacy, timing and the person’s task.

tabs.label: A relative’s help
tabs.body: A person may choose help. Requiring it because the service is inaccessible can reduce independence and expose private information.

tabs.label: A second version
tabs.body: A compliant alternate version has specific conditions under the rule. Have the responsible staff evaluate whether its use is permitted and effective.

check.question: Which claim about an inaccessible form is too broad?
check.correct: A phone number automatically resolves every digital-access requirement and communication need.
wrong: A phone option may help, but its effectiveness needs consideration.
Current communication duties can remain despite a web-rule exception.
The direct-access barrier may still need a lasting correction.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. A generic phone number does not automatically establish an effective or permitted alternative for every person and task.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the blanket claim. The other statements preserve the need to examine context, continuing duties and the actual barrier.

items.text: Can the person complete this task privately and within the relevant timeframe?
Any phone number proves full web compliance.
Is direct access technically or legally impossible under §35.202?
Which communication method works for the person in this context?
A relative must complete every inaccessible form for the person.
Does the alternative provide substantially equivalent or greater access under §35.203?

lessons.next: The final lesson organizes inventory, correction and verification while keeping formal exceptions and burden decisions with the proper authority.

scenario.context: A practice resident reports a form barrier. The team proposes a phone route that is available only after the person’s application deadline.
options: Examine an effective timely response with the responsible staff and track the lasting barrier correction.
Declare the task accessible because a phone number exists.
Tell the resident to ask a relative to submit private information.
responses: This addresses the current task and its timeframe while connecting the recurring issue to a proper correction process.
A route that misses the deadline does not establish effective access to the task.
The person may choose help, but imposed dependence is not an appropriate substitute for examining the access need.

lessons.transfer: Compare two practice response routes for a service task using effectiveness, timing, privacy and independence. Name any question requiring specialist or legal guidance.

move.control: You can connect a present need to the appropriate response and recurring repair.
move.failure: A generic workaround is called a completed solution without checking the task.
move.next: Ask the responsible staff whether the proposed route actually works for the person and context.

lessons.title: Plan correction and verify the result
lessons.summary: An inventory becomes useful when it leads to owners, repairs and supported conclusions about accessible tasks.
lessons.objective: Assign an owner, action and review point to a documented barrier.
objectives: Assign an owner, action and review point to a documented barrier.
Distinguish a planning priority from a formal exception or burden determination.
Write a scoped progress statement that does not overclaim complete compliance.
takeaways: Use priorities to organize work, not to declare low-priority people or tasks exempt.
Formal burden decisions require the authority, evidence and written reasons the rule specifies.
Verify corrected tasks and state what remains unchecked.
lessons.statement: A sound plan shows what will change, who will act and how the team will know the change works.

image.caption: A team’s plan is stronger when progress and unresolved questions are both visible.

intro.heading: Move from inventory to accountable action
intro.body:
An inventory can reveal hundreds of documents and several contracted tasks. A leader needs a workable plan, not a list that sits untouched. Group the work by current service use, reported barriers, upcoming changes and responsible owners. Use the agency’s accessibility and legal guidance to determine obligations and sequence actions. A priority order organizes effort; it does not turn a lower-priority item into an exception or excuse a present unmet communication need.

For each barrier, name the blocked task, responsible team, corrective step and review point. Include procurement or vendor involvement when needed. Check the final result after repair, including linked documents and confirmation steps. Avoid reporting that a whole service complies when only a small part was tested. State what was checked and what remains, then assign the next action.

The federal rule’s burden provision is specific. Under §35.204, a fundamental-alteration or undue-financial-and-administrative-burden decision belongs to the public entity’s head or designee, considers all resources available for the service, program or activity, and requires a written statement of reasons. The entity still takes other action that provides the benefits or services to the maximum extent possible without the alteration or burden. A team’s crowded schedule or limited local budget is not itself that formal determination. Minnesota’s own requirements and exception processes also need separate consideration.

In the practice DSD project, the leader reports verified form and document repairs, the remaining contracted step and its assigned review. This is honest progress. It does not claim an audit that did not occur or hide an unresolved barrier behind a percentage. Keep the plan current when content, technology, sources or legal requirements change.

inThisLesson: Verify and report the actual result.
lessons.keyStatement: A planning choice is not a legal exception, and a repair promise is not a verified result.

flashcards.back: A defined action with ownership, relevant support, timing and a check of the final task.
An order for organizing work. It does not by itself remove an applicable requirement.
A specific authorized decision under the rule requiring resource consideration and written reasons, with continuing action duties.
A report limited to the evidence actually obtained, including remaining barriers and unexamined areas.

accordion.heading: Check the plan before calling it ready

items.title: Ownership
items.body: Every connected step needs a responsible contact, including vendor or shared-team tasks. A referral is not the same as a completed correction.

items.title: Authority
items.body: Separate the team’s work sequencing from formal exemption, burden or legal decisions. Use the responsible office for those determinations.

items.title: Verification
items.body: Review the corrected task under relevant conditions and state the scope. Track recurring barriers after content or software changes.

tabs.label: Too broad
tabs.body: All services comply because twenty files were repaired. The conclusion exceeds the evidence and can hide unexamined tasks.

tabs.label: Too vague
tabs.body: We are working on it. This gives no action, responsibility or check point to people who need a result.

tabs.label: Useful
tabs.body: These tasks were checked and corrected; this remaining barrier has an owner and next review. The statement records progress and limits clearly.

check.question: A team’s local budget is low. Does that alone establish an undue-burden decision under §35.204?
check.correct: No. The specified authority must consider the relevant available resources and provide written reasons, with continuing duties under the rule.
wrong: Yes. Any team can declare every item exempt.
Yes, if the team labels its plan a pilot.
No review is needed once a vendor promises a future fix.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The formal provision is not a local convenience decision. Use the appropriate authority and preserve the rule’s remaining action requirements.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Distinguish work planning from a formal determination. A pilot label, local budget or vendor promise does not establish the rule’s conditions or a completed repair.

items.text: The team schedules the active application form for review first.
Does §35.204 apply under the required authority and resource assessment?
The corrected keyboard task was tested under the recorded conditions.
The owner and review date are assigned to the vendor issue.
Does an exception meet every relevant condition?
The final document’s reading order was checked and corrected.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to map one service, confirm the relevant requirements and assign a supported next action. Continue with the Minnesota standards and accessible-procurement courses where they match your responsibilities.

scenario.context: In this example, a team repairs two documents and leaves the contracted form untested. It wants to announce complete web compliance.
scenario.prompt: What should the leader approve as the progress statement?
options: Complete compliance, because the team made a good effort.
The verified document repairs, the untested form and its assigned owner and next review.
No statement at all until every possible issue is resolved.
responses: Effort matters but does not establish complete conformance. The conclusion is broader than the evidence.
This gives a supported account of progress and remaining responsibility without pretending the full service was verified.
A limited, honest update is useful. It can show completed work while preserving attention to what remains.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice progress statement with one verified repair, one unresolved task and one next review. Separate any formal decision from the team’s priority order.

move.control: You can make actions and evidence visible without overstating legal conclusions.
move.failure: A priority, percentage or promise is treated as proof of complete compliance.
move.next: Assign a specific owner and verification step to a connected service barrier.

jobAid.subtitle: A leader’s public digital-access review
remember: Use the current federal dates: April 26, 2027 and April 26, 2028 for the specified entity categories.
Minnesota’s digital standard effective July 1, 2024 remains separate.
Older documents still used for application or participation are not exempt merely because of age.
A technical exception does not erase continuing Title II duties. Formal conclusions belong with authorized officials.

sections.heading: Map and clarify
items: List the full public task, documents, apps and contracted steps.
Identify owners and the appropriate accessibility, procurement and legal contacts.
Use entity population, current source text and current agency guidance when planning dates.

sections.heading: Review and respond
items: Ask for task and technical evidence, including limits of automated checks.
Examine each exception’s actual conditions rather than applying a blanket label.
Arrange effective present access and examine timing, privacy and independence.

sections.heading: Correct and verify
items: Assign an owner, action and review point to each barrier.
Keep priorities distinct from formal burden or exception decisions.
Verify the final task and report only the progress supported by the evidence.
